The systematic gathering, recording, and analysing of data to answer about questions relating to marketing of goods and services.
It mainly relates to questions about a product’s: Positioning, or its Target Market
E.g. Do customers get use out of this new feature? What makes a customer buy a Macbook Air?What could we do to our product to make consumers use it more often?

These terms are used interchangeably to mean the same thing, although:
Market research tends to refer to investigating the likely market success of a product or service that is entering/changing positions in the market, whereas marketing research collects data to make decisions that are specific to decision-making about marketing and promotion.
Market research = is this product idea viable?
Marketing research = how do we construct the right marketing plan and marketing mix to increase sales?

1. Continuous process: every business is faced with problems and opportunities that change with the market conditions.
2. Wide scope: product research, market research, consumer research, promotion research, international market research, price research and distribution research.
3. Helps decision-making: Decisions based on experience and research are better than decisions based on intuition.

In marketing research, the consumer is the focal point.
However, con­sumer behaviour is difficult to judge precisely - it is a social science.
Due to this inherent nature, it suffers from certain levels of uncertainty and inaccuracy.

bme-y11-u1-marketing-research.title: Marketing Research - How to do it?

blocks.text:
A researcher has several options of research methodology.
Methods include:
Field survey method (surveys)
Observation method (watching consumers shopping)
Experimental research (setting up fake scenarios to observe consumer behaviour)
The selected method depends on time availability, funds, number of respondents to be covered, location of respondents and literacy levels etc…

~ 3 minutes ~
Write down 2 reasons (linked to Business Function!) that a company might choose to conduct some marketing research:

To make decisions about marketing that will enhance the success of the product.
Increases Sales
Increases Advertising Effectiveness (reducing the cost per purchase)
Increasing the Profit
Reposition the brand in the minds of the consumer
Improving Public Image
Navigate a competitor’s new threat
Customise the product / sales experience to better suit the target market

Primary research is data which is obtained first-hand. This means that the researcher conducts the research themselves or commissions the data to be collected on their behalf. Primary research means going directly to the source, rather than relying on pre-existing data samples.

Benefits:
Specific to the needs of the business
Owned by the business
Research process can be controlled
Disadvantages:
Expensive
Time consuming
Difficult to produce reliable results

Secondary research is data which is obtained from another source, from a pre-existing study. This means that the researcher was not conducted by the researcher themselves. Secondary research means using pre-existing data samples to draw insights into a business’ specific area of interest.

Benefits:
Quick to obtain results
Cheaper than collecting primary data
High Quality and reliable (if sourced from a professional marketing research firm)
Disadvantages:
NOT Specific to the needs of the business
NOT Owned by the business
Research process CANNOT be controlled
Secondary data may come from inside the business, like from another department, collected for another purpose, or it may come from an external source.

Benefits:
Quick to obtain results
Cheaper than collecting primary data
High Quality and reliable (if sourced from a professional marketing research firm)
Disadvantages:
NOT Specific to the needs of the business
NOT Owned by the business
Research process CANNOT be controlled

Collecting data is just the beginning, analysing it to draw insights is the most important step!
The process of inspecting, cleansing, transforming, and modeling data with the goal of discovering useful information, informing conclusions, and supporting decision-making.
Inspecting: scanning through to see what data was collected
Cleansing: removing errors, outliers etc.
Transforming: converting big data into a manageable and digestible form
Modeling data: creating trend and patterns

The marketing mix coordinates decisions about the offer and its delivery. Product decisions include features, branding and packaging. Positioning is how the business wants the target market to perceive the offer relative to alternatives.
A reusable bottle aimed at commuters might emphasise durability, a leak-resistant lid and convenient cleaning. Packaging and claims must support that position.

Skimming sets a relatively high initial price to capture willingness to pay before later adjustments. Penetration uses a low entry price to build demand. Psychological pricing influences perceptions, while premium or prestige pricing supports an exclusive position.
Choose a price using customer value, competition, costs and objectives. A low price that fails to cover relevant costs can increase sales while damaging profit.
Direct distribution connects the producer with the buyer. Indirect distribution uses intermediaries such as retailers or wholesalers. Location, convenience, delivery cost and reach affect the choice.

Advertising buys promotional space. Publicity attracts attention through coverage. Sales promotions provide short-term incentives. Personal selling uses direct interaction. Viral marketing encourages people to share content. A business needs a message and channel that suit the target market.

People includes employee training and customer service. Processes are the procedures through which customers obtain a product or service. Physical presence includes signage, a webpage and staff uniforms.

For a repair business, technically skilled staff, a clear booking process and a trustworthy website reinforce the same promise. A strong advertisement cannot compensate indefinitely for poor service delivery.

Evaluate the mix against objectives using sales revenue, sales returns and customer satisfaction. Sales returns can indicate quality, fit or expectation problems and should be interpreted alongside sales volume.

Example: sales rise from $40,000 to $46,000, an increase of 15%. If returns also rise sharply and satisfaction falls, the campaign may be attracting purchases that the product does not fulfil. Recommend a response using all three measures.
Even Coca-Cola uses segmentation to successfully sell it’s drinks to the market!

To get where you want to go - you need a plan!
A marketing plan is a document that shows how a business is planning to use advertising and promotional resources to target their specific target market and increase sales.
A new marketing plan will be written before each new promotional campaign, and it will have specific strategies in order to achieve specific goals!

Market Position
Competitor Analysis
Target Market Analysis
Marketing Goals
Marketing Strategy
Marketing Mix
Positioning refers to the place that a brand occupies in the minds of the customers and how it is distinguished from the products of the competitors.

Competitor Analysis is an assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of current and potential competitors.
This helps businesses to identify opportunities and threats.
Product (quality / choice)
Price
Positioning
Premises
People

A study of how well your product or service fits the needs / wants of the target market.
What do you know about them? (characteristics)
Have you asked them what they want/need?
Is this the right target market for your product?

Set SMART goals that the business wants to achieve from their marketing campaign.
This keeps the marketing team on track and accountable to meeting their overall objective, by setting individual goals.
E.g. Lunchtime sales in weekday metropolitan areas by 13% by 1 July 2023.
This is the most important section of the Plan, it refers to the specific actions the business is going to take in order to achieve its goals.

Link market position, competitor analysis, target market analysis, marketing goals, strategy and mix. Goals should be measurable and time-bound. SWOT distinguishes internal strengths and weaknesses from external opportunities and threats. Allocate responsibility, resources and measures for review.

In general, customer relationship management refers to the actions that a business takes in order to build and maintain positive customer relationships.
(This is not referring to CRM software, but rather the act of building and maintaining relationships).

Customer relationship management can occur during a variety of phases in the customers interaction with a business. These phases include:
Customer’s Initial Enquiry
Customer Interactions pre-purchase
Placing order / making purchase
Following up on a purchase
Billing (for orders)
After-sales service

bme-y11-u1-customer-relationship-managem.title: Customer Relationships are Built through Experiences

blocks.text:
The greater the number of positive customer experiences, the more likely the customer will be to:
Place an order/ make a purchase,
refer the product two friends and family (WoM)
make a repeat purchase (Brand Loyalty)
Leave a positive review (WoM, brand ambassador)
etc…

bme-y11-u1-customer-relationship-managem.title: Customer Relationships are Built through Experiences

blocks.text:
The greater the number of negative customer experiences, the more likely the customer will be to:
Speak badly about the business / product (WoM)
Purchase from another business (market share)
Leave a negative review (WoM, public image)
etc…

Pick a product/service that you had a terrible customer experience with.
What did you buy?
Why was the experience so bad?
Did you go through with the purchase, or pull out / demand a refund?
If you were asked to give the business a star rating - what would it be?
Would you purchase from this business again?

It is easier to sell more products / services to an existing customer, with whom your brand already has a relationship, rather than forging a relationship with an entirely new customer.
- leverages past experience with the brand
- easier to encourage purchase
- opportunities to sell products that complement the customer’s existing purchase

Increased Sales & Revenue
Increased Brand Loyalty
Decreased Advertising Spend required

bme-y11-u1-customer-relationship-managem.title: How to build and maintain customer relationships

blocks.text:
Relationships can be built with customers using a variety of means.
We are going to discuss two particular strategies including loyalty programs and early adopter incentives.

Some businesses decide to reward customer loyalty, to increase repeat purchase and build strong relationships with customers who may become ‘brand ambassadors’.
Brand Ambassadors are very useful as they increase positive word-of-mouth  about a business or a product and this leverages social sharing as a form of promotion.

Customer loyalty programs, or schemes, offer an incentive to customer to encourage repeat business.
This rewards customers each time they purchase and increases the likelihood that they will continue to purchase from the business.
E.g. points / discounts

In your notes, list one business that you have brand loyalty to.
Do you know of a loyalty program they run? If so, list it.
Are you a part of their loyalty program? If so, what do you get?
How do you feel when you get rewarded for using the program?
Does it influence your purchases in this industry? E.g. would you say your’re more likely to buy from them, over another competitor, if it’s available?
Does this make you more likely to recommend the product? Why or why not?

An early adopter is an early customer of a business, product, or technology.
They are one of the first buyers of the product or service, and they support the early sales required by the business to keep going. They also provide feedback and necessary feedback to shape development of the product for the general public.

Loyalty incentives encourage repeat custom, while early-adopter incentives encourage trial of a new offer. Evaluate retention, repeat purchase, service quality and cost. CRM also depends on reliable processes, trained employees and responsible use of customer information.

Early adopters are pioneers, and take more of a risk, because they don’t rely on the WoM of fellow consumers to feel comfortable buying the product, and the product may still contain bug/errors.
In fact, for many early adopters, the fact that they are first to purchase a product is an important part of their identity.

Businesses must reward early adopters, because the revenue from early adopters is critical in helping the business to establish itself in a given market.
Therefore, early adopter incentives are often given, to encourage early adopters to get on board.

The best example of early adopters is that of the first iPhone by Apple.
When it was first launched in 2007, the iPhone was priced at $600.
The price was quite high, as Apple lacked any experience in the industry.

An early adopter is likely to pay more for the product than later adopters, but accepts this premium if:
They become part of an exclusive list of customers that receive news, updates and product launch details before the general public
Have access to purchase ‘pre-released’ products, before they go on sale to the general public
Are asked to provide opinions and feedback on early versions of the product, to help shape its development.
Owning the product helps raise their social status.
They receive additional after sales service and support.
Their product comes with additional features or add-ons.

Digital marketing is the tools and strategies that use online based digital technologies and platforms to promote products and services.
In a world that is increasingly connected and operating online, marketers are taking advantage of a new digital marketplace where consumers are living.

Online advertising uses the internet to promote products and services to audiences and platform users.
This is particularly important in the digital age, where most consumers are connected to the internet 24/7, and many purchases even take place online.
E.g. Google Advertising, advertisements on the side of websites, pop-up video ads

In mobile phone application advertising, the advertisers pay the app developers to feature ads. These ads appear on apps which are viewed on mobile devices.
Many apps are free to download and even use, so advertising is a great way to monetise the app, without directly charging users for the benefit.
Brands are also able to access customer attention, while the customer is doing other things, like reading the news.

Pull up your Facebook or Instagram account.
What is the first ad you see?
How many ads do you see in the first 35 posts?
Is the ad relevant to your interests / likes or something you have been searching for or talking about?
How do you think they know you are interested in this product or service?
Compare the first ad you saw to a friend on the other side of the room.
What are the similarities?
What are the differences?

An e-newsletter is an electronic report containing news, information and offers from a business that is sent to its customers or subscribers.
This helps build relationships with the existing customer base, encourage repeat purchases and upselling and increases brand loyalty.
Sent to customers email address semi-regularly e.g. on a monthly or quarterly basis

The activity of electronically buying or selling of products on online services or over the Internet.
Australia is the 13th largest market for eCommerce with a predicted revenue of US$43,206.7 million by 2023.
Food & Personal Care is the largest market and accounts for 28.6% of the Australian eCommerce revenue. It is followed by Fashion with 25.4%, Toys, Hobby & DIY with 21.0%, Electronics & Media with 15.9%, and Furniture & Appliances with the remaining 9.1%.

Social media advertising describes forms of online advertising and digital marketing that leverages the power and connectivity of social networking services to promote goods and services.
Social media advertising and promotion can be both paid and unpaid.
E.g. Paid advertising on Facebook, an influencer sharing a post about a product, or sharing a post organically
